articles.title: Trump wants Smithsonian to build George Washington statue, exhibit
articles.summary: President Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution in late Friday social media posts to install a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington outside of its National Museum of American History (NMAH) and open an exhibit to honor the founding father. The president requested that the museum complex replace the “Infinity” statue, which has stood outside of the…
articles.body:
President Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution in late Friday social media posts to install a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington outside of its National Museum of American History (NMAH) and open an exhibit to honor the founding father.

The president requested that the museum complex replace the “Infinity” statue, which has stood outside of the NMAH since 1967, with one depicting the nation’s first president.

“That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“George Washington does,” he continued. “He is easily America’s Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist.”

Trump asked for work on the proposed, five-year exhibit to begin “now,” adding he wants to be open through Feb. 22, 2032 — the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birthday.

The president has repeatedly criticized Smithsonian leadership for promoting a “social justice” agenda and sought to direct changes to museum exhibits.

The Smithsonian operates independent of the White House, but its leadership is overseen by a Board of Regents — includes Vice President Vance, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, bipartisan lawmakers and a group of citizens.

This week, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he would step down from his role by the end of the year amid disputes with the Trump administration.

In July, Trump directed the installation of signage outside of the NMAH to warn visitors that some of the museum’s exhibits did not match his administration’s perspective on the nation’s past.

The president cited a July White House report that criticized Smithsonian leaders as “extreme” activists and concluded the NMAH “fails in the basic task of illuminating” U.S. history in its content.

The Trump administration also referenced this report when they threatened in September to cut federal agencies’ cooperation with the museum complex.

“Instead of focusing on ideological activism, the leaders of America’s taxpayer-funded, National History Museum should be focused on telling America’s story—fairly, accurately, and coherently—and there is no better person to start with than George Washington,” the president wrote in his Saturday Truth Social post.

The Smithsonian Institution did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed touts ‘whole a--’ medical credentials while defending sex changes for children
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, argues 'whole a--' doctors should decide trans treatment without government interference.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said the government should not restrict sex changes, arguing that "whole a--" doctors like himself should be allowed to make their own determinations for patients' treatment plans. The remarks came during El-Sayed's Friday rally held at Michigan State University, during which the former Detroit Health Department head responded to a student's question about protecting sex changes. Since launching his campaign, El-Sayed has flaunted that he is a "physician" and, if elected, he would be the first doctor to serve as a Democratic senator in 50 years. However, Fox News Digital previously reported El-Sayed has never held a medical license in Michigan or New York. "I went to a whole a-- medical school, everybody I graduated with also went to whole a-- medical school," El-Sayed said. "And then ... they went to whole a-- residency. Right? And some of them went to whole a-- fellowship. They took whole a-- exams to provide whole a-- healthcare." DEM SENATE HOPEFUL’S ‘PHYSICIAN’ CAMPAIGN PITCH UNDER FIRE AFTER LICENSE RECORDS REVEAL KEY GAPS "They are the experts that a patient wants to see when they seek care," El-Sayed continued. "And the decision about what healthcare is necessary ought to be held between a patient — and or their parents if they're under the age of 18 — and their doctor. That's it." The remarks come as the Trump administration has made major strides in restricting minors' access to "sex-rejecting" procedures, which include hormone therapy and surgeries. Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced that Mount Sinai had joined other hospitals, like Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic Foundation and Connecticut Children's Hospital, to halt sex change procedures for children after reaching an agreement with the Trump administration. MEDICAID ENDS FUNDING FOR CHILD SEX-CHANGE PROCEDURES AS TRUMP ADMIN SLAMS 'EXPERIMENTAL' TREATMENTS El-Sayed has made the promise of Medicare for All — government-run healthcare — as the major selling point of his campaign; he said that even though the government will be covering the bill, it needs to stay out of the doctor's decisions about a patient's treatment plan. "I don't think the government gets to have a say about what health care is provided in what circumstances and why," El-Sayed said. "And to me, that is the standard on which we decide how we make health care decisions." THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS "Not what the government says you can or can't do, but what a patient and/or their parent, if they're under 18, and their provider to decide. That's the most important thing," El-Sayed continued. "And there's a lot of disinformation about us, what we're talking about, when we talk about reproductive rights and when we're talking about health care for the trans folks. But, in the end, the place where the rubber meets the rope is in that clinical room between a patient and a provider, and that to me is the center we should engage on." El-Sayed argued that Republicans agree with his belief that treatment decisions should be between a patient and their doctor, pointing to the Right to Try Act, which allows terminally ill patients to try experimental drug treatments that aren't yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration after they have exhausted all other treatment options. "Because conservatives fought for a very long time for this legislation called 'Right to Try' legislation, which is the idea that the government couldn't tell you [that] you couldn't have a certain medication," El-Sayed said. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBE COULD UPEND WIDELY USED TRANSGENDER YOUTH TREATMENT GUIDELINES "So they agree that the decision about healthcare ought to be between the person and their provider. That's it. So let's use that standard, and keep to that standard, and make sure the government doesn't have the ability to tell you what you can or cannot do with your own life," El-Sayed said. However, the research on the efficacy of treating individuals with gender dysphoria by allowing them to change sexes with "cross-sex" hormones and puberty blockers is limited. The World Professional Association for Transgender Health, whose guidelines are used by leading medical associations like the American Academy of Peditatrics, is currently facing a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission stemming from allegations that its guidelines misled parents about the "medical consensus and medical necessity, as well as the safety and effectiveness" of sex change procedures. The FTC has accused WPATH of failing to disclose the side effects associated with some procedures, such as patients experiencing incontinence, erectile pain, mood disturbances, pelvic pain, and vaginal pain stemming from "cross-sex" hormones. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, countries that have socialized medicine have put restrictions in place for minors' seeking sex changes. In England, the National Health Service put a pause on "cross-sex" hormones for 16- and 17-year-olds in March after finding research was "really weak" to support it. The country already had a ban in place restricting children under 16 years old from taking sex-change hormones. El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding his medical credentials.

articles.title: $25 million in national park project funds blocked by Trump administration: Report
articles.summary: The Trump administration has reportedly blocked more than 130 planned projects at national parks across the country, putting more than $25 million worth of funding on hold. The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service (NPS), “disapproved” of agreements last month for projects at Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Joshua Tree and other parks, The Washington…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has reportedly blocked more than 130 planned projects at national parks across the country, putting more than $25 million worth of funding on hold.

The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service (NPS), “disapproved” of agreements last month for projects at Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Joshua Tree and other parks, The Washington Post reported, citing internal documents.

NPS often works with outside organizations for projects that require additional workers or specialized expertise rather than hiring additional federal employees, the Post added.

The outlet reported that the funding came from sources including congressional appropriations and existing federal programs and was awaiting the Interior’s approval before it could be released.

Interior spokesperson Aubrie Spady confirmed to The Washington Post that the department had rejected agreements with groups she described as “actively working against the best interests of the American people and the priorities of this administration.”

“This decisive action is ensuring that these taxpayer dollars are being used in alignment with the administration’s objectives to make life more affordable for Americans, unleash domestic energy production and expand access to our public lands,” she said.

Joshua Tree National Park in California was reportedly the most impacted, with at least 10 projects blocked, including wildfire preparation, burned area restoration and the removal of rodents that carry hantavirus from historic buildings.

Internal documents warned that losing funding for the projects could make it more difficult and costly to fight fires at the park.

“If this work is not completed, the park will be unable to fight wildfire. Fires will be larger and fire suppression will be more expensive,” the documents read, according to the Post.

Other projects would have worked to protect prehistoric Native American mounds in Iowa from falling trees, supported efforts to preserve an endangered snake species in California and paid for the care of sled dogs at Denali National Park and Preserve in Alaska.

The Great Basin Institute, a conservation nonprofit that works with federal land agencies, reportedly had more than 70 agreements worth at least $12 million rejected.

The group’s CEO, Peter Woodruff, told the Post that it was not directly notified by the Interior about the decision and did not know why its agreements had been blocked.

In July, President Trump notably signed orders reducing the size of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, prompting Patagonia and a coalition of Native American and environmental groups to challenge the reductions in court.

articles.title: 25 years after the anthrax attacks, we are still unprepared for biological warfare
articles.summary: When the nation desperately needs help, it will be from a government that has lost the ability to provide it.
articles.body:
In the early, chaotic days after the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks, five letters were dropped into a mailbox in Princeton, New Jersey, across from the Princeton University campus. Containing a coarse brown powder later identified as anthrax spores, the envelopes were addressed to media organizations, including NBC News and the New York Post.

By early October 2001, the phones inside New York City’s emergency operations center were ringing off the hook with demands for Cipro , the antibiotic used to prevent anthrax infection after exposure. Powerful politicians and government officials were calling. I remember the menace in one personal assistant’s voice: “The senator wants his Cipro. Now.”

They believed, with perfect conviction, that they were entitled to receive it first — and that I was the one keeping it from them. It got ugly fast.

I have often thought about those calls over the last 25 years, and here is what they taught me. Fear is a solvent. Firm convictions about masks and social distancing and vaccine safety dissolve when people believe that they, or their children, could die. Upon first contact with a deadly pathogen, Americans will not be divided over whether they want protection. They will be unanimous. But right now, there is nobody to provide it.

COVID-19 should have pulled us together, but it did just the opposite. Instead of learning the lessons and building back stronger, we spent the last six years pointing fingers at the institutions of government, as the institutions themselves have come apart. That is the perfect storm we have built. When the nation desperately needs help, it will be from a government that has lost the ability to provide it.

With her latest book, Annie Jacobsen shines a spotlight on this alarming vulnerability. “ Biological War ” takes a threat we all agreed to ignore and lays it out in riveting detail: the Soviet stockpiles of engineered pathogens, built to kill hundreds of millions in a matter of days; the proliferation of bioweapons labs around the world, creating yet more novel pathogens through high risk “gain of function” research.

The book is not alarmism; it is dispassionate reporting based on dozens of interviews with high-level political, governmental, medical and military experts. Its conclusions should stop us cold. The weapons to end civilization exist, they are more available than they have ever been, and the geopolitical environment has never been more conducive to their use.

The good news is that we don’t need a miracle to stop a pandemic; we just need epidemiologists to do their vital work — finding the sick and tracing their contacts to break the chain of transmission. Nothing more exotic than trained people, funded and in place before the first case appears.

The COVID crisis revealed major gaps in our ability to do this. Over the past 18 months we have shut down the U.S. Agency for International Development and proposed cutting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s budget. We walked out of the World Health Organization in January, surrendering our seat at the table where the world’s disease surveillance data is shared.

Here is the part that keeps me awake. No level of government could support the population at the speed and scale a major biological attack would demand. Not just to treat the sick, but to feed the people who cannot leave their homes, and to rapidly dispense preventive medications — oral antibiotics for anthrax or plague — through local points of dispensing.

We possess extraordinary scientific, medical, pharmaceutical research and logistics capabilities, but capabilities are not preparedness. Preparedness is capability organized for action, at speed, under pressure. That requires national coordination. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, the agency charged with this, has been cut, second-guessed and floated for relocation.

That is the agency Cameron Hamilton now inherits. His recent confirmation ends a long period of temporary leadership. Now he must be given the resources to build and the authority to act. This means a funded FEMA and a clear mission. It means public health and emergency management planning together before the event instead of in the middle of one. And it means the new administrator putting his agency in the room where biological threats are being tracked — not waiting to be invited after the outbreak has a name.

Call it civil defense. Call it whatever you want. We need a national effort — a sustained, funded, unglamorous program to rebuild stockpiles, strengthen disease surveillance and refresh and validate mass-prophylaxis plans.

Twenty-five years ago next week, a handful of envelopes sent people scrambling for protection. The next biological emergency will move faster, reach farther and demand infinitely more from the institutions charged with protecting us.

The threat is real. The system is blinking red. We need to be ready when the phones start ringing.

Kelly McKinney served as associate commissioner at the Department of Health during New York City’s response to the 2001 anthrax attacks and later as deputy commissioner of the New York City Office of Emergency Management.

articles.title: The one line from JD Vance’s GOP keynote that reveals his vision for America
articles.summary: JD Vance framed the midterm elections as a fight over every American child's birthright in a Dallas keynote that previewed his post-Trump GOP vision.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance used his keynote address at the Republican midterm convention Thursday to frame the November elections as a fight over America’s future, arguing that every child is entitled to inherit the country’s opportunities regardless of background. The speech also gave Vance one of his most prominent national platforms since becoming vice president to define his own political vision, as he emerges as a central figure in the GOP’s post-Trump future and speculation continues about a potential 2028 presidential campaign. "Every American child is born an heir, born with the right to inherit the blessings of the greatest country on Earth — not because of who their parents are, what they look like or where they come from, but because they are Americans and this is our country," Vance said in Dallas. "And that birthright, ladies and gentlemen, is what this November is all about," he added. VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP Vance tied that idea to his own family, speaking about the birth of his fourth child, Alec, six weeks ago. He said he wants his son and all American children to grow up with access to clean water, healthy food, a quality education, safe communities and the opportunity to afford a home and raise a family. He also connected that vision to the legacy of his late friend Charlie Kirk, who was killed one year ago. Vance said Kirk encouraged young men to fall in love, start families and become fathers. The speech marked a shift from the personal story of Vance’s Appalachian upbringing that he emphasized during the 2024 Republican convention. Instead, Vance presented himself as a father focused on the country his children will inherit, while using the platform to preview the issues and themes that could define his future in the Republican Party. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE Vance then pivoted from his family-focused message to a sweeping attack on the Democratic Party. He accused Democrats of abandoning working-class Americans and becoming increasingly hostile toward the country’s traditional values. "The Democrats are the party of hatred," Vance said. "They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it." FOLLOW FOX NEWS DIGITAL’S COVERAGE OF THE GOP’S 2026 MIDTERM CONVENTION He urged Republicans to view the November election as more than a traditional partisan contest. "This November is so much more than red team versus blue team," Vance said. "It’s about fighting for our fellow citizens, for their dreams, and for the inheritance of a great nation that all of us are going to leave behind." articles.title: Graham accepts debate with Andrews after challenger pushes for more
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) announced Friday she plans to debate her Democratic challenger in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews, ahead of November’s elections. “I’m in,” Graham wrote in a social media post. “On October 11, I will take the debate stage and expose Annie Andrews’ radical positions she’s spent the last year hiding…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) announced Friday she plans to debate her Democratic challenger in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews, ahead of November’s elections.

“I’m in,” Graham wrote in a social media post . “On October 11, I will take the debate stage and expose Annie Andrews’ radical positions she’s spent the last year hiding from South Carolina families.”

“This is your seat, South Carolina, and it will be my honor to show you why I am ready to continue serving you and representing our conservative values in Washington,” she continued.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) tapped Graham to fill out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate term after his death in July . President Trump quickly backed the late senator’s sister for a full term.

In the state’s Republican primary runoff in August, Graham beat Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) to become the GOP’s nominee in this race.

The Oct. 11 event, hosted by local public broadcaster SCETV, will mark Graham’s first public debate since her primary face-off with Norman last month. The appearance caused some to doubt the incumbent’s qualifications after she flubbed a national security question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

“I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham responded, before adding, “But I do support the military.”

Andrews, who has repeatedly challenged the Republican nominee to participate in a debate, responded to Graham’s announcement on Friday evening.

“Darline’s primary debate performance left voters with serious questions about whether she is prepared for this job,” the Democrat said in a statement shared on social media.

“Voters deserve to see us side by side and judge for themselves,” she continued. “I’m eager to finally see Darline on the campaign trail and show South Carolinians exactly why I’m the best person to fight for them in the United States Senate.”

Andrews previously launched an unsuccessful bid for the U.S. House in 2022. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates South Carolina’s Senate race as “Solid Republican.” The state’s voters supported Trump in the past three presidential elections.

articles.title: Bill Maher rips Macklemore's Gaza stance, says celebrity 'moral confusion' is fueling antisemitism
articles.summary: Bill Maher targeted Macklemore on Rosh Hashanah for calling the Gaza war a genocide, arguing that the claim fuels a global rise in antisemitism.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher spent the first night of Rosh Hashanah taking aim at Macklemore and other anti-Israel celebrities, arguing that calling the war in Gaza a genocide is fueling a global rise in antisemitism. During Friday night’s episode of HBO’s "Real Time," Maher first criticized members of the Democratic Party who have spoken out against Israel during the Israel-Hamas war. "Because nowhere has this moral confusion become more obvious than in a place called Gaza," Maher said. "A little strip of land that was not part of the original Israel, but they won in a war launched against them, but then gave back, gave back as a peace gesture — did they tell you that part on TikTok, kids?" BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH' Maher then turned his attention to Macklemore — whose real name is Benjamin Hammond Haggerty — after the musician repeatedly made calls to "Free Palestine" while performing his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall" as an opening act for Ed Sheeran at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, earlier this month. "I think Macklemore spoke for all clueless celebrities when he said, ‘I know enough to know this is a genocide,’" Maher continued. "Actually, you don't know s---. It's not. It's not a genocide. It's a counterattack in a war." MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER The "Thrift Shop" rapper made headlines in early September for his comments about the Israel-Hamas war while on stage at the concert, where he wore a keffiyeh as he delivered his message to the crowd. "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine," Macklemore said. JERRY SEINFELD GIVES BLUNT THREE-WORD RESPONSE TO INFLUENCER ASKING FOR A 'FREE PALESTINE' "I said, ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," he continued. Fox News Digital reached out to Macklemore's representatives for comment. Maher continued criticizing Macklemore and other liberal figures, disputing their assertion that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza in response to Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack. "Gaza equals genocide is a lie, an easily provable lie," Maher said. "And the fact that so many prominent Democrats go along with it is, to me, the party's worst moment since they undid Reconstruction after the Civil War. Democrats are policing their candidates really hard on this issue. Say it — say it's a genocide. Say it." PROMINENT HOLOCAUST MUSEUM CHALLENGES MAMDANI WITH OFFER IN RESPONSE TO CLAIMS ABOUT 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA Maher concluded his "New Rule" segment by arguing that what he described as false claims about the war have contributed to the rise of antisemitism. "If you're one of the many people these days asking, ‘This explosion of antisemitism around the world that we see, where is it coming from?’" Maher said. "This. This is where it's coming from. Because if you really think someone is committing genocide, of course you have full permission to hate them. And history shows, for whatever reason, when it comes to hating the Jews, people don't need a lot of permission." GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS Macklemore’s comments also drew criticism from Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, who told Fox News Digital that the rapper's public stance on Israel represents a "calculated risk." "Take a political stance and most celebrities can count on alienating half their audience," Mudd said. "That's the easy math. The harder split is what's left: about a third thinks you should stay in your lane and entertain, and only a third is glad you used your platform to say it." "It's fine, if you're making a calculated risk," he continued. "Using your platform to influence politics is a decision that can affect your fans' support, your reputation, your career, and your future earnings, so know the risk before you make it." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Mudd concluded his comments by suggesting that Macklemore should take into account the potential consequences of taking such a polarizing stance as a public figure. "There's no rule against entertainers taking a stance, but he needs to understand the career, reputational and pushback risk that comes with it."

articles.title: Trump plots a campaign blitz; GOP candidates face a decision
articles.summary: President Trump’s upcoming midterm campaign blitz is risking dragging down Republicans facing tough reelection bids as his approval rating plummets ahead of November. Trump will head to battleground North Carolina to campaign with Senate nominee Michael Whatley on Wednesday in an effort to boost Republican efforts in the fight to keep the seat red. The…
articles.body:
President Trump’s upcoming midterm campaign blitz is risking dragging down Republicans facing tough reelection bids as his approval rating plummets ahead of November.

Trump will head to battleground North Carolina to campaign with Senate nominee Michael Whatley on Wednesday in an effort to boost Republican efforts in the fight to keep the seat red.

The visit is slated to be the first of many for Trump, as Republicans seek to nationalize the midterm elections.

However, other Republican incumbents and candidates are choosing to keep Trump at arm’s length, as candidates figure out how the president factors into their own political calculus.

“I think he’s putting everyone in a very tricky situation. Do you stump with him and literally and figuratively embrace high gas prices and war in Iran, or do you snub him and risk him telling the base not to show up for you?” said one Democratic strategist.

“This week made clear he wants everyone to act as though he’s on the ballot and given his approval ratings that’s bad news for Republicans, even in traditionally red areas,” the strategist continued.

This past week’s Republican midterm convention served to provide a jolt of energy to the GOP base ahead of November. Republicans are facing historical headwinds going into the midterms, given the party in the White House normally loses seats in the House and the Senate during the first two years of an administration.

On top of that, recent polls show Trump’s approval rating continuing to decline. A recent Focaldata/Financial Times poll released showed Trump’s approval rating hitting a new low of 32 percent.

Despite those negative polls, Trump and the White House are imploring his base of supporters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot, arguing a Democratic majority will be a blow to the president’s agenda. Trump’s allies note that there are members of his political base only he can motivate to head to the polls.

Trump sought to galvanize the base during the two-day convention by vowing to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans keep their majorities. He also led an unusual convention pledge meant to convince GOP voters to get out of the house and to the polls to vote in the midterms.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” the president told supporters. “You know that, OK? You go to hell, and I don’t want that to happen to you. So please go and vote, because together we will defeat the communists.”

Beyond Trump, Republicans also expect Vice President Vance to get out on the campaign trail. They might be looking more forward to that, pointing to his energetic speech at the convention Thursday evening.

“Vance has been and will continue to be another fantastic surrogate on the trail, especially in a place like Ohio where he remains the most popular person statewide. He’s able to reach voters where they’re at across the Midwest and beyond,” said one Republican operative.

While getting the base to turn out at higher levels than in past midterm elections could give Republicans a boost, Democrats argue the strategy of using Trump to turn out the base could backfire on swing voters unhappy with the direction the country is headed.

“I do think there’s value in reminding voters he promised to lower costs and keep us out of war. He’s done the opposite and they have a right to feel betrayed,” the Democratic strategist said.

Still, a lot of Republicans facing tough reelection bids are not showing any signs of shying away from the president.

Reps. Mike Lawler (N.Y.), Scott Perry (Pa.), Monica De La Cruz (Texas), Derrick Van Orden (Wis.), Ryan Mackenzie (Pa.), and Rob Bresnahan (Pa.) were among the House Republicans facing tough reelection bids who attended the party’s two-day convention in Dallas.

On the Senate side, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), and Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chair, were among the Senate candidates in competitive races who attended the convention.

“The energy behind the president and his policies was on full display at the Republican convention, and our candidates will be carrying that momentum and enthusiasm into their districts,” one GOP source told The Hill. “We’re going to put the president and his achievements on the ballot as much as possible and highlight what’s at stake in this election.”

One Republican strategist noted that the party ecosystem has not done enough over the past two years to promote the policy wins of the administration and congressional Republicans, including provisions seen inside the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts.

“If I had a critique, people don’t know what’s been done,” the strategist said. “I don’t think the public relations has been maybe as aggressive or as effective as it should have been.”

“You look across districts and you have folks who work in service jobs where they rely on tips or they rely on overtime, where you have a senior population, or where you have families that are relying on the expanded child tax credit,” the strategist continued.

Lawler is one of eight Republicans to have one reelection in 2024 in a district carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris. While the Republican lawmaker has at times broken with the administration, most recently on comments Trump made about the Iran war , he has still embraced the president publicly.

Trump traveled to Lawler’s district in May to appear alongside the congressman in a campaign-style event. Lawler also spoke at this past week’s midterm convention, introducing the family of Sherida Gorman, a college student who was shot and killed in Chicago earlier this year, in an emotional tribute. The Trump administration has stated the man accused of killing Gorman, Jose Medina, of entering the U.S. “through the open door policy” of the Biden administration.

“I think that’s a great example of the real-life impact of policy,” the Republican strategist said. “We can talk about policies very esoterically from 30,000 feet, and I think what you see in that instance is the trickle down of bad policy into changing a family’s life.”

Other Republicans facing tough reelection bids made the decision not to attend the convention, including Reps. Tom Barrett (Mich.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan.

“It’s a case-by-case basis,” the Republican strategist said. “Whether or not you’re seen on the campaign trail with the president or whether you’re not seen with him or the administration, the other party is going to tie you to that administration.”

“You might as well get the benefit of it,” they added.

articles.title: JD Vance was right to stand by Tucker Carlson — and free speech
articles.summary: ance not only chose loyalty over political expediency, he demonstrated that he was one of the few “adults in the room” on the international stage.
articles.body:
For those who have not been paying attention, members of the media, certain Republicans and defenders of both Israel and the Jewish faith have been marching upon the White House with rhetorical pitchforks and torches, demanding that Vice President JD Vance publicly renounce his friendship with “ the monster,” Tucker Carlson.

The three main drivers of that demand revolve around accusations that Carlson is either antisemitic, anti-Israel or anti-Trump. And the accusations are getting louder by the day.

Anyone who has even casually followed Vance’s relatively short tenure as vice president is aware that rather than avoiding controversial issues, he often likes to dive right in and mix it up. And when a reporter brought up the topic at a recent gathering in the White House press room, the loaded question presented him with just such an opportunity.

“Everybody knows that Tucker Carlson and I are friends,” the vice president calmly retorted. “And I think it’s very obvious that Tucker has said some things that I disagree with.”

Vance then added something that demonstrated his character and resolve: He made it clear that despite the growing pressure, he was not going to cut and run from a friendship. “I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them,” he said.

Washington has become a place where throwing friends “under the bus” is not only a regular occurrence, but it has also evolved into an art form. Vance not only chose loyalty over political expediency, but he demonstrated that he was one of the few adults in the room on the international stage.

He did so by stressing a truth that desperately needs to be repeated in every corner of our fractured nation: “If you have a disagreement with someone politically — even over a deeply held issue — you should still be friends with that person,” he said, “because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.”

Bingo. I have long believed that God gave us two ears and just one mouth for a reason. We learn more from listening than from shouting.

In the age of Trump, many members of the media have proclaimed themselves part of the “resistance.” Most on the left are burrowing deeper and deeper into partisan silos. Listening is not high on these people’s list of priorities. And the same self-destructive behavior holds true for many in the MAGA and conservative worlds.

Hate, denunciation and willful ignorance are sadly three of the most corrosive toxins spreading across a republic that recently celebrated its 250th anniversary .

And that brings us back to Carlson, who has repeatedly claimed to his almost 18 million followers on X that the U.S. no longer exists in principle, or is no longer a functioning democracy. Love him or hate him, agree or disagree, Carlson spoke a belief that rings true for millions of Americans fearful for the future wellbeing of our nation.

So who carries the day? Is it Vance, who says that we had better debate it “because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another ?” Or is it those doing everything in their power to cancel dissenting voices?

In the 1995 movie “The American President, ” fictional President Andrew Shepherd, played by Michael Douglas, storms to the podium in the White House press room to state an important truth: “America isn’t easy. America is advanced citizenship. You gotta want it bad, ’cause it’s gonna put up a fight. It’s gonna say ‘You want free speech? Let’s see you acknowledge a man whose words make your blood boil, who’s standing center stage and advocating at the top of his lungs that which you would spend a lifetime opposing at the top of yours.'”

Vance gets that. He has known since his massively dysfunctional childhood that “America isn’t easy.” He knows that Carlson’s voice makes the blood of other Americans “boil.”

But he also believes in Carlson’s constitutionally protected right to free speech. More than that, it can be safely assumed that Vance believes if you have a reasoned argument to counter Carlson, then you should make it, passionately but civilly.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Surrogate who fled to Texas to avoid abortion appeals custody case to Supreme Court
articles.summary: The surrogate who fled to Texas after the unborn child’s biological parents requested she have an abortion is asking the Supreme Court to intervene in the custody battle — which garnered national attention and state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) intervention. McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday asking the high court to temporarily block…
articles.body:
The surrogate who fled to Texas after the unborn child’s biological parents requested she have an abortion is asking the Supreme Court to intervene in the custody battle — which garnered national attention and state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) intervention .

McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday asking the high court to temporarily block a California court order recognizing Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar as the 4-week-old child’s legal parents.

West gave birth to the boy on Aug. 12 in Dallas and named him Gabriel. The California couple, who are the child’s biological parents, instead called him Rumi.

The pair asked West to have an abortion after discovering the then unborn child was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a serious condition in which the left side of the heart is underdeveloped and unable to properly pump blood throughout the body.

The baby’s doctors recommended three after-birth surgeries as the standard treatment for the condition, and he underwent the first of several planned surgeries after his birth, according to the filing.

The custody fight began after doctor’s discovered the condition during the pregnancy. Ahmed and Gilkar asked West to have an abortion, but she refused. West later traveled to Texas, where she sought custody and the ability to make medical decisions for the child.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) intervened in the case , demanding protection for the surrogate mother and arguing the child should receive the medically necessary treatment.

A Texas judge subsequently ordered the hospital to provide life-saving care, appointed a guardian and prohibited the child from being removed from the state.

But on Sept. 1, the Texas court recognized a California judgement establishing Ahmed and Gilkar as the infant’s parents and dismissed West from the case with prejudice, according to her filing. The surrogate says she is now unable to receive information about the child or participate in decisions related to his medical care.

West’s attorneys are asking the Supreme Court to put the California judgment on hold while they seek further review, arguing it lacked jurisdiction.

West also says she fears the child could be taken to California and placed in hospice care instead of receiving additional treatment. Her filing says the child could be moved as soon as Sept. 17.

Ahmed and Gilkar have maintained they are the child’s parents. Gilkar previously told a Texas court the couple considered abortion after learning of the diagnosis but later decided to continue the pregnancy.

articles.title: Ex-mayor found liable for alleged sexual assaults of 7 women, ordered to pay $13M
articles.summary: Dominic Foppoli, former Windsor, California, mayor, faces a punitive damages phase after a jury awarded seven women $13 million in sexual assault case.
articles.body: The former mayor of a small town in northern California was found civilly liable Friday for allegedly sexually assaulting seven women. Dominic Foppoli, who led the town of Windsor from late 2018 to 2021, was ordered to pay a combined $13 million in compensatory damages. The payouts to the women, whose allegations span from 2001 to 2020, will range from $6,000 to $4,650,938 each, KTVU FOX 2 reported. He could also have to pay punitive damages to the women. That phase of the civil trial will begin on Tuesday. Foppoli has consistently denied all wrongdoing and has never been criminally charged in connection to the allegations. He stepped down as mayor in May 2021 after four women came forward to the San Francisco Chronicle to accuse him of sexual assault. FORMER NJ DEM MAYOR ALLEGEDLY DRUGGED, SEXUALLY ASSAULTED CHILD HE MET ONLINE The lawsuit, filed in April 2022, detailed allegations from seven Jane Does. Several women alleged Foppoli drugged their drinks before assaulting them, while Jane Doe 1 claimed he raped her dozens of times, including one alleged incident in which she said he handcuffed her to a bed. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, a total of 13 women have accused Foppoli of sexual assault or misconduct. In 2024, the state attorney general’s office suspended its criminal investigation into Foppoli, saying prosecutors did not have enough evidence to warrant filing charges on the cases not barred by the statute of limitations at that time. Foppoli testified during the civil trial, which began in July, again denying the allegations against him. "I've been a terrible boyfriend and partner, cheating, selfish and egotistical, but I've never done any of those things I'm being sued for," Foppoli said on the stand, according to KGO Eyewitness News. The jury also found the Santa Rosa chapter of Active 20-30, an all-male charitable social club where Foppoli was a member, liable for Jane Doe 4's alleged assault and awarded her an additional $2 million, the Chronicle reported. FBI AGENTS CONFRONT SWALWELL AT AIRPORT IN NEW FOOTAGE AS VIEWERS ZERO IN AND PILE ON According to the lawsuit, the woman alleged Foppoli sexually assaulted her during the national Active 20-30 convention in Reno, Nevada, in June 2012. She also accused the organization of failing to investigate complaints she made to its leaders. Traci Carrillo, an attorney for the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital that the initial San Francisco Chronicle story "gave some of our clients a voice that no local news agency wanted to touch because it accused a powerful and connected local politician of crimes and sexual misconduct." "It took over 5 years to get them justice, which was always about accountability. Their trauma was real, and they were believed, not shamed or silenced in the courtroom," Carrillo added. "They feel vindicated and will now focus on the much-needed healing the jury has provided for them." Foppoli's attorney, Andrew Watters, said in a statement to Fox News Digital that he would seek a mistrial over claims that the court improperly excluded key witnesses for the defense. If that fails, Watters said he would pursue an appeal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "What happened with the verdict was that the jury sent a message based on questionable self-reported evidence and junk science, and that’s not appropriate. It appears the passions of the jury were inflamed by the evidence, and they hated my client, so they made a very large award to punish and make an example of him," Watters said in a statement. Foppoli, speaking at a press conference outside the courthouse Friday, said his accusers "are trying to crucify me for a cause I'm not responsible for," adding that they were motivated by the $13 million payout. Foppoli still faces a separate lawsuit from Farrah Abraham, a social media influencer and former reality television personality who claims the ex-politician raped her in March 2021 at a house party in Florida. That civil case is expected to go to trial next year, according to court records. The Chronicle reported that Christopher Creek Winery, which Foppoli owns, settled a separate lawsuit filed by a Montana woman who alleged Foppoli raped her multiple times in 2020 when she was 18.

articles.title: Blue state governor's pardon of convicted felon torpedos a major Supreme Court immigration fight
articles.summary: Kathy Hochul pardoned a convicted noncitizen, effectively mooting a Supreme Court case on bond hearing rights for detained immigrants facing deportation.
articles.body: The Supreme Court will no longer hear an oral argument for a case centered on bond rights for noncitizens detained for lengthy periods, ruling the case moot after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul pardoned a lawfully present Dominican citizen, who pleaded guilty to second-degree assault. Hochul pardoned Keisy Guerrero Mariano, who is identified in court documents as "Keisy GM," in late August, effectively killing the Trump administration's appeal to the Supreme Court arguing that noncitizens, including those with green card status, do not have a legal right to a bond hearing for a prolonged detention if they have committed crimes that are grounds for mandatory deportation. Hochul, who is staunchly opposed to President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement crackdown, issued the pardon for Mariano just as the brief was due. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT Solicitor General John Sauer agreed Friday that Genalo v. Black is now moot, but said the Trump administration will seek an "alternative vehicle" to challenge the Second Circuit’s 2024 ruling that prolonged immigration detention can trigger a constitutional right to a bond hearing. Sauer said the administration intends to find another case through which the Supreme Court can resolve the issue during its 2026-27 term. The lawsuit centered on the challenges of plaintiffs Carol Williams Black, a Jamaican national with lawful standing, and Mariano — both convicted criminals detained by ICE. APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS Mariano was first arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in 2020 over a 2015 second-degree assault conviction for which he served time, making him eligible for deportation. He spent nearly two years in ICE detention, but was released in 2022 due to a nationwide injunction that required the release of detainees because of COVID-19 health risks. Prior to his release, Judge John P. Cronan of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Mariano's habeas corpus request in November 2021. But in May 2024, the Second Circuit overruled Cronan's decision, ruling that the government must grant noncitizens a bond hearing once detention becomes "unreasonably long." Failure to do so, the court ruled, would violate the Fifth Amendment's due process clause. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case June 15; however, the high court ruled Black's case moot because he had left the United States and filed a court declaration that he would not be returning to the country. Black was convicted in New York in 2000 of sexually abusing a minor under the age of 11. DHS BLASTS MINNESOTA BOARD FOR UNANIMOUSLY PARDONING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CONVICTED OF 3 ASSAULTS Hochul's decision to issue a pardon to Mariano has garnered fierce criticism from legal experts. "Pretty wild to fully pardon an aggravated felon to (1) stop the felon from getting deported and (2) stop the Supreme Court from ruling on an issue. (Especially as this litigation has been going on for years)," Eric Wessan, Iowa’s solicitor general, posted on X. He praised Sauer's decision to fight back on the Second Circuit's ruling. "I wonder how many non-American felons Governors like Hochul will choose to fully pardon and free to avoid them facing consequences for their actions," Wessan added. articles.title: Dem handlers lash out when Ramaswamy staffer confronts their boss about debate: ‘No pictures’
articles.summary: Video shows Amy Acton's campaign staff confronting a cameraman who asked why she refuses to debate Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor race.
articles.body: Campaign personnel for Amy Acton, Ohio’s former health director and Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, got into a confrontation with a Republican political activist wielding a camera last Saturday at one of Acton’s campaign events in Harrison, Ohio. When the cameraman approached Acton, asking her why she continued to decline invitations to debate her Republican challenger, Vivek Ramaswamy, her staff quickly rushed in to block him off from Acton. The video, which shows Acton walking away from the interviewer, adds to criticisms from Ramaswamy’s camp that she hasn’t given a good answer for why she isn’t willing to do a debate as both candidates enter the homestretch of their campaigns. articles.title: America’s doctor shortage is a national security threat
articles.summary: The United States faces a projected deficit of approximately 187,000 physicians by the mid-2030s due to a federal residency funding cap established in 1997.
articles.body:
If you plan on breaking a leg or contracting anything more complicated than a mild head cold by the mid-2030s, you might want to reconsider.

The U.S. is barreling toward a deficit of roughly 187,000 physicians over the next decade. Nearly half of that gaping hole exists in primary care, the basic, front-line medicine that keeps people out of emergency rooms. A country that leads the world in medical innovation is facing a future where seeing a doctor for a routine checkup could feel like winning the lottery.

The standard, lazy policy fix for this crisis involves raiding other nations for their medical talent. For decades, American health systems have treated foreign medical schools as an offshore supply chain, pulling doctors out of developing countries to cover the gaps in rural Kansas and inner-city clinics. This is not a wise policy, and it’s certainly not sustainable.

Treating the global South as a farm system for American hospitals is ethically bankrupt and strategically brain-dead. Foreign medical schools often operate with vastly different clinical baselines, lower funding levels, and questionable accreditation oversight compared to the rigorous training grounds of the U.S. Attempting to bridge those structural gaps through bureaucratic rubber-stamping compromises quality control across the healthcare system.

During the 1970 public health panics, lawmakers assumed global talent streams would flow forever without disruption. But this assumption no longer holds. A single pandemic, localized conflict, or sudden shift in immigration policy leaves American waiting rooms completely empty. A nation of 330 million people cannot subcontract its physiological survival to the diplomatic climate of overseas states.

American medical training remains the absolute global gold standard. Johns Hopkins, Harvard, and Mayo Clinic do much more than teach medicine. They invent the protocols. They run the trials and set the baseline standards that the rest of the planet copies. When you land in an intensive care unit, you want a physician trained under the most rigorous, high-resource academic framework in human history. Throwing away that competitive advantage by refusing to build enough seats for your own citizens is pure institutional incompetence.

The bottleneck is concerning. It is also entirely artificial, engineered by a 1997 federal policy decision that froze Medicare funding for graduate medical education. The Balanced Budget Act of 1997 capped the number of residency slots the federal government would subsidize, locking the pipeline in place while the American population grew and aged.

Thousands of brilliant, highly qualified American college graduates apply to medical school every single year, only to be turned away. They possess the test scores. They have the drive and the ambition, yet they hit a brick wall created by quarter-century-old federal accounting tricks. The U.S. created a system where it rejects its own talent, then acts shocked when it runs out of personnel.

Fixing this problem requires treating physician production as a quite literal life-or-death matter. We view microchips, steel and aerospace engineering as vital domestic infrastructure that cannot be outsourced without massive national security risk. Human bodies are the ultimate critical infrastructure, and a country that cannot heal its own population is inherently vulnerable.

When a biological strain mutates, or a systemic crisis hits, foreign supply chains collapse instantly. A nation dependent on external talent for basic domestic healthcare operates with a massive structural target on its back.

Uncorking this bottleneck means lifting the 1997 Medicare residency cap immediately and expanding state-funded medical schools. It means offering direct, full-tuition coverage for domestic students who agree to practice primary care in underserved American counties for a decade. The U.S. throws billions of dollars at defense contractors for military hardware every year without as much as blinking; funding 20,000 new medical residency slots costs a fraction of a single stealth bomber program.

Elected leaders need to treat the production of American-educated doctors with the exact same urgency historical planners reserved for the Manhattan Project or the Apollo program. Those massive mid-century mobilizations succeeded because policymakers recognized that survival depended on training domestic talent and building national capacity.

A superpower capable of splitting the atom and putting human beings on the moon should not be defeated by the simple task of training enough physicians to care for its own citizens. The choice is clear: America can act now, or it can watch a preventable shortage mutate into a full-scale healthcare emergency that leaves millions waiting for care when they need it most.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Trump political adviser is ‘cautiously optimistic’ about GOP in upcoming midterms
articles.summary: A top political adviser to President Trump said he is “cautiously optimistic” that Republicans can keep control of Congress in November, despite political headwinds for the party and the president’s sinking approval ratings. “I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November,” James Blair told NBC News’s…
articles.body:
A top political adviser to President Trump said he is “cautiously optimistic” that Republicans can keep control of Congress in November, despite political headwinds for the party and the president’s sinking approval ratings.

“I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November,” James Blair told NBC News’s podcast, “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition.” “But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history.”

Blair served as White House deputy chief of staff until April, and now oversees MAGA Inc., the Trump-aligned super PAC that is expected to spend heavily on the midterms.

His comments come as Republicans face an unfavorable political environment ahead of the midterm elections, as recent polling shows voters souring over Trump’s job performance, specifically his handling of the economy and the deeply unpopular Iran war.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Friday showed voters would rather see Democrats regain control of the House over Republicans, if the midterms were held now.

Blair acknowledged the challenges, but argued that Republicans still have time to plead their case to voters.

“There is a national backdrop against which things are being fought, and there are local considerations and sort of very specific considerations that a good campaign will be able to utilize both of,” Blair said.

As part of their midterm strategy, Republicans are working to ramp up the turnout of GOP voters ahead of November.

Trump closed out the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday by asking supporters to pledge to vote and bring their friends and family to the polls.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” Trump joked . “So please go and vote.”

Blair said Trump is particularly helpful in turning out people who supported him in the 2024 presidential election but do not regularly vote in midterms.

“Democrats are already using him as a turnout tool for their voters, whether Republicans do that or not,” he said.

Blair further downplayed concerns about the political impact of the six-month Iran war and on concerns about the economy, saying the Trump administration is dealing with inflation that he blamed on former President Biden.

“We’re still cleaning up that mess, and we need more time to finish the job,” Blair said. “That’s what we’re asking for in November.”

MAGA Inc. has been spending its large cash reserves on key races. Trump said last month that he had raised about $850 million and planned to spend “a lot” of the money helping Republicans win their elections.
